Researchers followed 200 university students for one semester to study the link between sleep and exam results. Students who slept at least seven hours on the nights before exams scored on average eight percent higher than those who slept less than six hours. The effect was strongest in subjects that require memorising facts, such as biology and history. The authors caution that stress may cause both poor sleep and poor results, so the study does not prove cause and effect.

The first bicycles, built in the early nineteenth century, had no pedals: riders pushed themselves along with their feet. Pedals attached to the front wheel appeared in the 1860s, which led to the high-wheeled penny-farthing, fast but dangerous. The safety bicycle of the 1880s, with two equal wheels and a chain drive, finally made cycling practical for ordinary people. Together with pneumatic tyres, it triggered a cycling boom that changed how people travelled and even contributed to women's independence.

Productivity, measured by completed projects, stayed the same, while sick days fell by a third. The company has decided to keep the four-day week but will review it again after one year.

Supporters say urban bees benefit from the variety of flowers in parks and gardens and are exposed to fewer pesticides than bees in the countryside. Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor but are home to about a quarter of all marine species. When water temperatures stay high for several weeks, corals expel the algae that live in their tissues and give them their colour and much of their food. This process, called bleaching, leaves the coral white and weak. If temperatures return to normal quickly, corals can recover, but repeated heatwaves make recovery increasingly unlikely.

From there it reached Europe several hundred years later, where it eventually replaced parchment and made the printing revolution possible.

La bicyclette de sécurité des années 1880, avec deux roues identiques et une transmission par chaîne, a enfin rendu le vélo pratique pour les gens ordinaires. Lorsque la température de l'eau reste élevée pendant plusieurs semaines, les coraux expulsent les algues qui vivent dans leurs tissus et qui leur donnent leur couleur et une grande partie de leur nourriture. Ce phénomène, appelé blanchissement, laisse le corail blanc et affaibli. Si les températures redeviennent rapidement normales, les coraux peuvent se rétablir, mais des vagues de chaleur répétées rendent ce rétablissement de moins en moins probable.

Pendant des siècles, la technique est restée un secret chinois. Elle s'est répandue dans le monde islamique au VIIIe siècle, où des villes comme Bagdad ont construit des moulins à papier. De là, elle a atteint l'Europe plusieurs siècles plus tard, où le papier a fini par remplacer le parchemin et a rendu possible la révolution de l'imprimerie.
